title: Detection of Social Media Accounts
summary: This detection strategy covers the reconnaissance technique of gathering social media account information, where an adversary builds a picture of employees, their roles, their connections, and their habits from public profiles. It matters because that picture supports highly targeted phishing, impersonation of a manager, and help desk social engineering that can reset a password. The telemetry that makes detection possible is web proxy and resolver logs showing access to social platforms from corporate devices, platform audit records where the organization has an official presence, and endpoint records of automation or scraping frameworks. The main failure mode is that ordinary staff use these sites constantly, so volume alone is meaningless unless you can isolate automated retrieval and correlate it with later targeting.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for signs that someone is collecting details about your staff from social media. Social media are public websites where people share posts, job roles, and connections. The rule watches for automated reading of many profiles in a short time. It also watches for access to these sites from servers and service accounts.
beginner.whyItMatters: A profile tells an attacker who reports to whom and who handles money. That makes a fake message far more convincing. Attackers also copy photos and writing style to impersonate a manager. If you see the collection, you can warn the staff who were studied.
howItWorks: The web proxy records each request to a social platform, with the user and the page.
The resolver records lookups for social platform host names from internal hosts.
The rule counts profile page requests per session and counts the different people viewed.
It flags sessions that come from servers, service accounts, or automation tools.
Platform audit records show bulk downloads where the company has an official page.
A single session reading many employee profiles in a short time raises an alert.
beginner.example: Picture a visitor book at a school gate. A parent who signs in to collect one child is normal. A visitor who signs in and then asks to see the class lists for every year group is not. The book shows the pattern, and the office staff ask a question.
takeaways: Automated retrieval of many profiles is the useful signal, not site visits.
Servers and service accounts have no reason to read social platforms.
Public collection from outside your network leaves no trace, so coverage is partial.

objectives: Explain what social media account information gives an attacker.
Identify proxy, resolver and platform records used for this detection.
Write a rule that flags bulk profile retrieval from one session.
Describe how to baseline normal social platform use at work.
Explain the privacy limits of monitoring staff browsing.
dataSources: Web proxy logs recording requests to social platform profile and search paths with user, user agent and session timing
Recursive DNS resolver logs for social platform host names queried by servers and service accounts
Social platform audit logs for bulk export or follower listing activity on organization owned pages
Endpoint process creation records for browser automation and scraping frameworks launched on managed hosts
logic: The pattern is one session retrieving an unusually high number of employee or organization profiles, or requests to social platform profile paths coming from a server, a service account, or an automation framework. The fields that must be correlated are the requesting identity or host, the session identifier, the count of distinct profile pages, the user agent string, and the time window. The malicious case is a short session that views dozens of employee profiles including job titles and contact details, especially from a host that never browses the web. The benign case is a recruiter or sales user reviewing a handful of profiles for work, from a normal workstation, in a session that also includes unrelated sites.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Bulk Social Platform Profile Retrieval From One Session
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: proxy
# detection:
#   selection:
#     r-dns|contains:
#       - 'social-platform-a[.]com'
#       - 'social-platform-b[.]com'
#     cs-uri-stem|contains: '/in/'
#   filter_approved:
#     cs-user-agent|contains:
#       - 'Approved Recruiting Tool'
#     src_host|startswith: 'vdi-'
#   condition: selection and not filter_approved | count() by session_id > 40 within 15m
# level: low
falsePositives: Recruiters and sales teams that research candidate or customer profiles as part of their normal role
Marketing staff who schedule and check company page posts throughout the working day
Approved social listening tools that collect public brand mentions from a documented service address
tuningNotes: Baseline profile request counts per user and per business unit for a month, then set the threshold above the busiest legitimate user and filter approved recruiting and social listening tools by user agent and source range. Scope the rule to servers, service accounts, and non office devices where social platform traffic has no business reason, and add a separate lower priority path for human users. The coverage you lose is genuine employee browsing, which will still generate volume alerts, and none of this helps when the collection is done from a personal device outside your network.
